questions.stem: A dying client tells the nurse that a specific family ritual should occur immediately after death and asks that several relatives be present. The request differs from the unit's usual practice. What is the best nursing response?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Explain that unit routine takes precedence over cultural or religious requests after death because consistent workflow is necessary for equitable treatment of all families on the unit.","B":"Clarify what the client and family specifically want, document those preferences, and coordinate reasonable accommodations that are safe and consistent with law and facility policy.","C":"Assume the request represents the standard practice of everyone from the same cultural group and apply the same ritual automatically to other clients from that background.","D":"Delay discussion until after death because discussing rituals in advance may increase distress and does not contribute meaningfully to individualized end-of-life planning."}}
questions.rationale: Culturally responsive end-of-life care begins with the individual's stated preferences rather than assumptions about a cultural group. The nurse should clarify and document the request and work with the interdisciplinary team to accommodate it when consistent with safety, law, and institutional requirements.
questions.source_name: National Institute on Aging — Providing Care and Comfort at the End of Life
questions.source_detail: Individualized end-of-life care should elicit and respect patient/family preferences and cultural or religious practices when they can be accommodated safely and lawfully.

questions.stem: A client with acute pulmonary edema is prescribed IV furosemide. The client has chronic kidney disease and baseline hearing impairment. Which administration concern is most important for the nurse to recognize?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Rapid IV administration increases the risk of ototoxicity; the nurse should use the prescribed controlled rate and monitor for tinnitus or worsening hearing.","B":"Rapid IV administration primarily increases the risk of severe hyperkalemia, so potassium replacement should be withheld until the infusion is complete.","C":"The client's hearing history is unrelated to furosemide because ototoxicity occurs only with oral therapy and is not associated with IV administration.","D":"Giving the IV dose rapidly is preferred because faster delivery lowers the risk of volume depletion and renal dysfunction while preserving the same diuretic effect."}}
questions.rationale: Furosemide labeling warns that tinnitus and reversible or irreversible hearing impairment have been associated with rapid injection, high doses, renal impairment, and other ototoxic drugs. IV administration should therefore follow the recommended controlled rate, with added vigilance in a client who already has renal and hearing risk factors.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Furosemide Injection
questions.source_detail: Current labeling warns that rapid IV injection, high doses, and renal impairment increase ototoxicity risk; controlled IV administration is recommended.

questions.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease is newly prescribed lisinopril. Which laboratory monitoring is most important after initiation and during dose adjustment?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Monitor serum calcium and magnesium because ACE inhibition most commonly causes clinically important hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia after initiation.","B":"Monitor serum potassium and renal function because lisinopril can cause hyperkalemia and clinically important changes in kidney function, especially in CKD.","C":"Monitor hemoglobin A1c and fasting glucose because ACE inhibition commonly causes treatment-limiting hyperglycemia during the first several weeks of therapy.","D":"Monitor bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase as the principal routine safety tests because predictable cholestatic injury is the main dose-limiting effect of lisinopril."}}
questions.rationale: Lisinopril labeling specifically advises periodic monitoring of renal function and serum potassium. Pre-existing kidney disease increases the importance of this surveillance because ACE inhibition can produce changes in renal function and hyperkalemia.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Lisinopril Tablets
questions.source_detail: Current lisinopril labeling: monitor renal function periodically and monitor serum potassium for hyperkalemia.

questions.stem: A client with a life-threatening fungal infection is receiving conventional amphotericin B and has a mildly elevated baseline creatinine. Which trend should the nurse prioritize during therapy?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A progressive rise in bilirubin with stable creatinine is the expected dose-limiting toxicity, so renal and electrolyte monitoring can remain routine.","B":"A fall in fasting glucose is the characteristic toxicity of amphotericin B and should be treated as the earliest marker of treatment intolerance.","C":"A rising creatinine with potassium or magnesium depletion is concerning for amphotericin-associated nephrotoxicity and requires close clinical review.","D":"New mild leukocytosis with unchanged renal function is the principal expected toxicity and usually determines whether amphotericin B must be discontinued."}}
questions.rationale: Conventional amphotericin B is nephrotoxic and its labeling recommends frequent renal monitoring, especially in patients with reduced renal function. Renal adverse effects include azotemia and hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia is also reported. Renal and electrolyte trends are therefore central to safe monitoring.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Amphotericin B for Injection
questions.source_detail: Labeling warns of nephrotoxicity, reduced renal function, hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia and recommends frequent renal-function monitoring.

questions.stem: A client receiving central parenteral nutrition has glucose values rising from 130 to 260 mg/dL over 24 hours. The central-line site is clean and the client is afebrile. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The glucose rise does not by itself establish a catheter bloodstream infection because hyperglycemia and central-line infection require separate clinical assessment.","B":"The glucose rise can be ignored because parenteral nutrition does not cause clinically important hyperglycemia unless the client had diabetes before admission or severe illness.","C":"The central line should be removed solely because glucose has increased, since hyperglycemia is considered a direct diagnostic marker of catheter infection.","D":"Parenteral nutrition can contribute to hyperglycemia, which should be monitored and managed; central-line infection risk is addressed separately with meticulous catheter care."}}
questions.rationale: Parenteral nutrition can cause or worsen hyperglycemia because it provides substantial intravenous carbohydrate. Hyperglycemia requires monitoring and management, but it is not by itself diagnostic of a catheter-related bloodstream infection. Central venous access carries an independent infection risk that is reduced through evidence-based line care.
questions.source_name: ASPEN — Parenteral Nutrition Care Pathway and Hyperglycemia Guidance
questions.source_detail: ASPEN guidance treats glycemic monitoring/management and central venous access safety as distinct components of parenteral nutrition care.

questions.stem: A client with prolonged profound neutropenia after hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation is cared for in a protective environment. A visitor brings fresh flowers and washed packaged fruit. Which nursing response is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Do not bring fresh or dried flowers or potted plants into the protective environment; handle food according to safe-food practices and the transplant program's policy.","B":"Reject both the flowers and every form of fresh produce because national infection-control guidance prohibits all uncooked fruits and vegetables for every neutropenic client.","C":"Allow the flowers because plant restrictions apply only to immunocompetent clients, while protective-environment patients have no special environmental fungal risk.","D":"Permit both gifts without review because protective-environment precautions address airborne isolation only and do not include environmental controls for fungal exposure."}}
questions.rationale: CDC protective-environment guidance prohibits fresh or dried flowers and potted plants for HSCT patients because plants can harbor fungal organisms. This does not support a blanket national rule banning every raw fruit or vegetable for every neutropenic patient; food handling should follow evidence-based food-safety and transplant-program policy.
questions.source_name: CDC — Isolation Precautions: Protective Environment
questions.source_detail: CDC Protective Environment recommendations prohibit fresh/dried flowers and potted plants for HSCT patients; food restrictions should follow the program's evidence-based policy.

questions.stem: A client with a coronary stent takes clopidogrel and is newly prescribed a proton-pump inhibitor. Which medication combination should prompt the nurse to clarify the plan because of a documented interaction?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Clopidogrel with pantoprazole, because all proton-pump inhibitors inhibit CYP2C19 to the same degree and are equally contraindicated with clopidogrel.","B":"Clopidogrel with omeprazole or esomeprazole, because these drugs can reduce formation of clopidogrel's active metabolite and diminish platelet inhibition.","C":"Clopidogrel with famotidine, because H2-receptor antagonists routinely block clopidogrel activation and are specifically prohibited by current labeling.","D":"Clopidogrel with calcium carbonate, because antacids irreversibly inactivate clopidogrel and eliminate antiplatelet activity for the entire dosing interval."}}
questions.rationale: Clopidogrel requires CYP2C19-mediated bioactivation. Current labeling advises avoiding concomitant omeprazole or esomeprazole because they significantly reduce exposure to clopidogrel's active metabolite and reduce platelet inhibition. The interaction is not identical across all acid-suppressing therapies.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Clopidogrel Tablets
questions.source_detail: Current labeling advises avoiding omeprazole and esomeprazole because CYP2C19 inhibition reduces active metabolite exposure and antiplatelet effect.

questions.stem: During a regional anesthetic procedure, a client develops sudden circumoral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste, dizziness, and agitation shortly after local anesthetic administration. What should the nurse suspect?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A predictable local anesthetic effect that confirms adequate nerve blockade and does not warrant escalation unless the injection site becomes painful or swollen.","B":"A simple anxiety reaction unrelated to the local anesthetic because neurologic symptoms are not recognized early manifestations of systemic local anesthetic exposure.","C":"Local anesthetic systemic toxicity, a potentially life-threatening complication that can progress from neurologic symptoms to seizures or cardiovascular collapse.","D":"An isolated vasovagal episode because tinnitus and circumoral numbness specifically indicate transient vagal stimulation rather than systemic drug toxicity."}}
questions.rationale: Neurologic symptoms such as circumoral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste, agitation, dizziness, and seizures can be early manifestations of local anesthetic systemic toxicity. LAST can progress to cardiovascular instability or collapse, so recognition must be prompt and the emergency response protocol activated.
questions.source_name: ASRA Pain Medicine — Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity Checklist
questions.source_detail: ASRA identifies LAST as a rare, life-threatening local-anesthetic complication requiring rapid recognition and response.

questions.stem: During general anesthesia after succinylcholine exposure, a client develops rapidly rising end-tidal CO2, generalized muscle rigidity, tachycardia, and metabolic acidosis. Which medication should the team prepare as the specific therapy for the suspected condition?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Naloxone, because the pattern is most consistent with opioid-induced hypoventilation and opioid reversal is the specific treatment for rising carbon dioxide and rigidity.","B":"Protamine, because the pattern is most consistent with excessive anticoagulation and heparin reversal rapidly treats the associated hypermetabolic physiology.","C":"Flumazenil, because the pattern is most consistent with benzodiazepine oversedation and reversal of GABA-mediated sedation corrects the muscle rigidity.","D":"Dantrolene, because the findings after a known triggering agent are characteristic of malignant hyperthermia and require immediate MH-specific treatment."}}
questions.rationale: Rapidly rising end-tidal CO2 and muscle rigidity after exposure to succinylcholine or a volatile anesthetic are classic warning signs of malignant hyperthermia. MHAUS recommends immediate malignant-hyperthermia treatment including dantrolene and discontinuation of triggering agents, with aggressive supportive management.
questions.source_name: MHAUS — Malignant Hyperthermia Treatment Recommendations
questions.source_detail: MHAUS identifies dantrolene as the specific treatment for an acute malignant-hyperthermia event and recommends continued monitoring for recurrence after initial control.

questions.stem: After routine vaccination, an adolescent says they feel well and wants to leave immediately. There is no history that requires an extended allergy observation period. Which instruction best reflects current CDC practice?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Remain seated or lying safely for about 15 minutes because observation helps prevent injury from syncope and allows prompt assessment if an immediate reaction occurs.","B":"Remain for 30 minutes after every vaccine because every recipient has the same allergy risk regardless of vaccine type, allergy history, age, dose number, or clinical factors.","C":"Leave immediately because routine post-vaccination observation is unnecessary for adolescents unless the vaccine was administered during an inpatient admission.","D":"Remain for several hours because standard observation is intended to capture most systemic vaccine adverse effects before the client is allowed to leave."}}
questions.rationale: CDC recommends observing most vaccine recipients for about 15 minutes after vaccination, with particular attention to preventing injury from syncope. Some vaccine-specific allergy situations call for longer observation, but a universal 30-minute or multi-hour observation period is not required for routine vaccination.
questions.source_name: CDC — Vaccine Administration: After Giving Vaccine
questions.source_detail: CDC recommends about 15 minutes of observation for most vaccine recipients, especially to reduce injury related to syncope; some specific allergy situations warrant longer observation.

questions.stem: A client taking warfarin says, 'I'm going to start eating a very large spinach salad every day even though I rarely eat leafy greens now.' Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Avoid every food containing vitamin K for the duration of warfarin therapy because complete elimination is necessary to keep the INR within the therapeutic range.","B":"Keep vitamin K intake reasonably consistent and discuss major dietary changes with the anticoagulation team because large changes can alter warfarin effect and INR.","C":"Increase vitamin K intake sharply whenever the INR is elevated because dietary vitamin K should be used by the client as an unsupervised method of reversing warfarin.","D":"Dietary vitamin K has no clinically meaningful interaction with warfarin, so the client can change intake abruptly without considering the anticoagulation plan."}}
questions.rationale: Warfarin labeling advises a normal balanced diet with a consistent amount of vitamin K and warns against drastic dietary changes such as suddenly eating large quantities of green leafy vegetables. The goal is consistency, not elimination of vitamin K, and major changes should be coordinated with INR monitoring.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Warfarin Sodium Tablets
questions.source_detail: Updated labeling advises maintaining a consistent vitamin K intake and avoiding drastic dietary changes that can alter INR and anticoagulant effect.

questions.stem: A client who cannot assist with transfers weighs more than the safe working load of the unit's standard mechanical lift. Which action best protects both the client and staff?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use the standard lift with additional staff stabilizing the client because exceeding the rated load is acceptable when several trained workers are present for the transfer.","B":"Perform a coordinated manual lift with enough staff because manual lifting is safer than delaying care while equipment with a higher load rating is obtained.","C":"Obtain mechanical equipment rated for the client's weight and dimensions and use trained staff according to the facility's safe-patient-handling plan for the transfer.","D":"Avoid repositioning or transferring the client until body weight falls below the standard lift limit because pressure-injury risk is lower than staff-injury risk."}}
questions.rationale: Safe patient handling requires equipment that is appropriate for the patient's weight, dimensions, mobility, and clinical condition. Equipment should never be used beyond its rated capacity. Facilities should have processes for obtaining bariatric-capable devices and trained assistance rather than relying on manual lifting.
questions.source_name: OSHA — Safe Patient Handling in Healthcare
questions.source_detail: OSHA safe-patient-handling principles support use of appropriate mechanical equipment and avoiding hazardous manual lifting; equipment must be suitable for the patient and task.

questions.stem: A nurse provides brief care to a hospitalized client receiving sealed-source brachytherapy. Which approach best applies basic occupational radiation-protection principles?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Stay as close to the radiation source as possible because distance has little effect on exposure once a sealed brachytherapy source is implanted in the client.","B":"Use gloves and a standard isolation gown as the principal radiation protection because routine barrier PPE provides equivalent protection to dedicated shielding in this setting.","C":"Avoid all necessary nursing care until the radioactive source is removed because there is no safe method for trained staff to care for a brachytherapy patient.","D":"Minimize time near the source, maximize distance when care permits, and use the shielding and radiation-safety procedures specified by the facility for this treatment."}}
questions.rationale: The NRC describes time, distance, and shielding as core methods for minimizing occupational radiation exposure. Staff caring for hospitalized brachytherapy patients must also receive facility-specific radiation-safety instruction, including safe handling, shielding, patient control, visitor control, and emergency notification procedures.
questions.source_name: U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission — Radiation Protection Principles and Brachytherapy Safety Instruction
questions.source_detail: NRC radiation protection uses time, distance and shielding; personnel caring for hospitalized brachytherapy patients require specific radiation-safety instruction.

questions.stem: An older adult receives a sedative-hypnotic at night and has a history of getting up unassisted when confused. Which nursing plan best addresses the medication-related fall risk?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use an individualized fall-prevention plan that addresses assisted toileting, environment, monitoring, medication review, and supported mobility based on the client's risks.","B":"Keep the client on strict bed rest with scheduled observation throughout the hospitalization because sedative exposure makes even closely supervised mobility unsafe for this client.","C":"Discontinue the prescribed sedative without contacting the prescriber because any medicine associated with falls must be stopped immediately by nursing staff.","D":"Use a bed alarm as the primary intervention because an electronic warning adequately replaces assessment of toileting, cognition, medication effects, and mobility."}}
questions.rationale: Fall prevention is most effective when interventions are tailored to the patient's specific risks. Sedating medications, cognition, toileting needs, environment, mobility, and supervision should all be considered. A single universal intervention, permanent immobility, or unilateral medication discontinuation is not appropriate.
questions.source_name: AHRQ — Fall TIPS: Patient-Centered Fall Prevention Toolkit
questions.source_detail: AHRQ fall prevention uses assessment of individual risks followed by a personalized prevention plan and consistent implementation.

questions.stem: A hospitalized client is placed in a restraint for a nonviolent safety indication after less-restrictive measures fail. The family asks, 'Exactly how often must every hospital reassess this restraint?' Which response is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Federal rules require the same once-per-shift reassessment interval for every restraint type and patient, so state law and facility policy cannot require closer monitoring.","B":"Monitoring and reassessment must meet CMS, state, and facility requirements and the client's condition; there is no universal q1–2h interval for every restraint.","C":"Once an order is written, nursing reassessment is unnecessary until the restraint causes an injury, the client requests removal, or the restraint order expires.","D":"Every restraint requires the same 15-minute documentation interval until discharge because monitoring requirements do not vary with indication or clinical context."}}
questions.rationale: CMS requires restraints to be used only when necessary, with ongoing monitoring, assessment, and discontinuation as soon as they are no longer needed. Requirements differ by context, including special rules for violent or self-destructive behavior, and state law or facility policy may be more specific. A single national q1–2h interval should not be taught as universal for every restraint.
questions.source_name: CMS — Hospital Conditions of Participation: Patient Rights, Restraint and Seclusion
questions.source_detail: CMS establishes ongoing monitoring and patient-rights requirements, including special one-hour face-to-face evaluation rules for violent/self-destructive restraint, while detailed monitoring intervals also depend on context and policy.

questions.stem: An acute-care inpatient is colonized with MRSA and is on Contact Precautions. The family asks when the precautions can be stopped. Which explanation is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Contact Precautions should stop automatically after 24 hours without fever because duration depends only on systemic symptoms and not on persistent colonization or transmission risk.","B":"A single negative nasal culture is a universal national criterion for stopping Contact Precautions because one test reliably confirms permanent clearance of MRSA carriage.","C":"CDC recommends Contact Precautions for MRSA in acute care, but the optimal discontinuation point remains unresolved; the facility's infection-prevention policy should guide removal.","D":"Colonization without infection never requires Contact Precautions in acute care because CDC limits this intervention to clients with active MRSA disease and draining wounds."}}
questions.rationale: CDC currently recommends Contact Precautions in acute-care settings for patients colonized or infected with MRSA. CDC also states that the duration and criteria for discontinuing Contact Precautions for MDRO colonization remain unresolved because carriage can persist and surveillance cultures can miss intermittent shedding. Facility infection-prevention policy should therefore guide discontinuation.
questions.source_name: CDC — MRSA Infection Control and MDRO Management
questions.source_detail: CDC recommends Contact Precautions for MRSA-colonized/infected acute-care patients and states that timing for discontinuation remains an unresolved issue.

questions.stem: Before right-knee surgery, the consent is correct but a whiteboard note lists the left knee. Who should perform the required site marking under current Joint Commission guidance?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Any staff member who notices the discrepancy may mark the site after checking the consent because site marking does not need to remain linked to procedural accountability.","B":"The patient should mark the site alone because involvement of the practitioner could bias the verification process when conflicting documentation exists.","C":"An unlicensed assistant may mark the site independently as long as a nurse later checks the mark during the final time-out immediately before incision.","D":"The licensed practitioner accountable for the procedure should mark the site, involving the patient when possible; limited delegation is allowed under defined policy."}}
questions.rationale: Joint Commission guidance updated in 2026 states that the site is marked by the licensed practitioner ultimately accountable for the procedure and who will be present when it is performed. Limited delegation may occur under defined supervisory/collaborative circumstances, and the patient should be involved whenever possible.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission — Universal Protocol: Site Marking
questions.source_detail: 2026 Joint Commission FAQ: accountable licensed practitioner marks the site; limited delegation is permitted in defined circumstances; patient involvement is expected when possible.

questions.stem: An emergency department has had several incidents involving aggressive visitors, especially when staff work alone in poorly visible hallways. Which prevention strategy best aligns with OSHA guidance?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use a violence-prevention program with hazard assessment, de-escalation training, reporting, security controls, and measures that reduce isolated work when feasible.","B":"Ask staff not to report threats that do not cause injury because documenting lower-level events increases administrative workload without improving prevention.","C":"Rely mainly on individual staff confidence because formal training, environmental design, security planning, and staffing practices do not materially affect violence risk.","D":"Encourage staff to approach escalating visitors alone so other patients are not alarmed and security is used only after an actual physical assault occurs."}}
questions.rationale: OSHA identifies working alone, poor environmental design, inadequate security, and lack of staff training and policies as healthcare workplace-violence risks. Recommended controls include a formal prevention program, worksite analysis, hazard controls, training to recognize and de-escalate violence, reporting, and security/environmental measures.
questions.source_name: OSHA — Workplace Violence in Healthcare
questions.source_detail: OSHA identifies working alone and inadequate security/training as risk factors and recommends comprehensive workplace-violence prevention programs with training and hazard controls.

questions.stem: A container of an unfamiliar cleaning chemical spills in a clinical work area and staff do not know its hazards. Which initial response is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Continue routine work around the spill until symptoms develop because a spill that appears small does not require hazard identification or protective measures.","B":"Stop the task, keep people away from the exposure area as appropriate, alert the facility response system, and use the SDS and trained spill procedures before cleanup.","C":"Clean the spill immediately with bare hands and paper towels because rapid removal is safer than waiting to identify the substance or obtain appropriate protective equipment.","D":"Evacuate the entire building for every chemical spill regardless of substance, quantity, ventilation, exposure risk, or the facility's hazardous-material response plan."}}
questions.rationale: OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard requires employees to have access to hazard information, labels, Safety Data Sheets, and protective procedures. Unknown chemical spills should be managed through the facility's trained hazardous-material/spill response, with exposure control based on the chemical and circumstances. Automatic building evacuation is not the correct response to every minor spill, and untrained cleanup is unsafe.
questions.source_name: OSHA — Hazard Communication and Hazardous Chemicals in Hospitals
questions.source_detail: OSHA requires hazard communication, SDS access, employee training and appropriate protective measures for hazardous chemicals; spill response depends on the substance and exposure conditions.

questions.stem: A nurse manager wants to improve a unit with low morale and inconsistent quality-improvement participation. Which leadership behavior best reflects a transformational approach?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Set all goals alone, discourage staff input, and use corrective discipline as the main method for obtaining compliance with unit expectations and improvement targets.","B":"Avoid setting a shared direction and allow each staff member to define independent priorities because leader involvement can reduce professional autonomy and creativity.","C":"Articulate a shared vision, invite staff ideas, develop team members, and connect quality-improvement work with meaningful patient and professional outcomes.","D":"Focus mainly on short-term rewards for task completion without mentoring, shared purpose, learning, or participation in how the unit improves care processes."}}
questions.rationale: Transformational leadership is characterized by a compelling shared purpose, development and empowerment of team members, support for learning and innovation, and alignment around better organizational and patient outcomes. Modern nurse-leader competency frameworks likewise emphasize leading people, influencing systems, collaboration, learning, and professional development.
questions.source_name: AONL — Nurse Leader Core Competencies
questions.source_detail: AONL's contemporary nurse-leader competency framework emphasizes leading people, influencing systems, professional development, collaboration and organizational outcomes.

questions.stem: Two nurses disagree about how aggressively to mobilize a client who recently fell. Both have clinically relevant information, and the disagreement is beginning to disrupt the team. Which approach is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Avoid discussing the disagreement so each nurse can follow a separate plan during their own shift, reducing interpersonal tension even if care becomes inconsistent.","B":"Have the more senior nurse make the decision without reviewing the other nurse's concerns because hierarchy is the preferred method for resolving informational conflict.","C":"Escalate immediately to formal disciplinary action against one nurse before attempting a structured discussion because unresolved clinical disagreement is misconduct.","D":"Use a structured collaborative discussion to share the concern and evidence, seek agreement, and create one patient-centered plan addressing mobility and fall risk."}}
questions.rationale: AHRQ TeamSTEPPS treats differing views about the care plan as informational conflict that should be resolved before it compromises quality or safety. Structured tools such as DESC, CUS, the Two-Challenge Rule, huddles, and collaborative discussion help teams focus on evidence, shared goals, and a mutually workable patient-centered plan.
questions.source_name: AHRQ TeamSTEPPS — Conflict in Teams and DESC
questions.source_detail: TeamSTEPPS recommends constructive conflict-resolution tools and collaboration to reach a safe, mutually acceptable solution centered on patient and team goals.

questions.stem: A nurse completes a comprehensive assessment of a newly admitted client and identifies several abnormal findings. Before selecting nursing interventions, which action best reflects the next step of the nursing process?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Begin implementing interventions immediately because once assessment data are collected, selecting nursing diagnoses can wait until after the first round of care is completed.","B":"Analyze the assessment findings to identify the client's nursing problems or diagnoses before selecting measurable outcomes and interventions for the individualized care plan.","C":"Set measurable outcomes first and then decide which assessment findings support them, because planning goals should precede interpretation of the client's collected data.","D":"Evaluate whether the care plan was effective before defining the problem, because evaluation is the step that determines which diagnosis should be assigned to the client."}}
questions.rationale: The nursing process begins with assessment. ANA describes diagnosis as the next step, in which the nurse analyzes assessment data and makes clinical judgments about actual or potential client responses. Outcomes/planning and implementation follow that problem identification.
questions.source_name: American Nurses Association — The Nursing Process
questions.source_detail: ANA describes the sequence Assessment → Diagnosis → Outcomes/Planning → Implementation → Evaluation.

questions.stem: A unit wants to reduce catheter-associated infections. A colleague proposes copying a protocol from a previous hospital without reviewing the local problem or evidence. Which action should the nurse take first in an evidence-based practice process?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Adopt the colleague's prior protocol immediately because a practice that worked elsewhere can be treated as sufficient evidence without defining the local clinical question.","B":"Search broadly for articles before clarifying the population, intervention, comparison, or outcome, because the research question can be written after implementation begins.","C":"Formulate a focused clinical question that defines the practice problem and desired outcome, then use that question to guide the evidence search, appraisal, and change process.","D":"Change the unit policy first and collect outcome data later because evidence-based practice begins with implementation rather than with a structured clinical question and search."}}
questions.rationale: Evidence-based practice begins by clearly defining the practice problem and asking a focused, answerable clinical question. A structured question such as PICO then guides the search, critical appraisal, implementation decision, and outcome evaluation rather than substituting anecdote or immediate policy change for evidence.
questions.source_name: Evidence-Based Practice Framework — Focused Clinical Question / PICO
questions.source_detail: Evidence-based practice uses a focused clinical question to guide the search and appraisal of evidence before practice change.

questions.stem: A client with a new stroke needs nursing care, physical therapy, nutrition planning, and discharge-resource coordination. Which approach best reflects effective interprofessional collaboration?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Bring the nurse, therapist, dietitian, social worker, and client together around shared goals, with each discipline contributing expertise while client preferences shape the plan.","B":"Ask each discipline to create an independent plan without discussing priorities with the others, because separate professional judgment reduces the risk of interdisciplinary bias and conflict.","C":"Assign one discipline to coordinate every aspect of treatment and ask the other disciplines to follow that plan, even when their assessments identify competing patient needs.","D":"Exclude the client from team planning until professionals reach agreement, because patient preferences should be considered only after the interdisciplinary plan is finalized."}}
questions.rationale: TeamSTEPPS identifies communication, team leadership, situation monitoring, and mutual support as core skills for high-performing health care teams. Effective interdisciplinary care coordinates different professional expertise around shared patient-centered goals and includes the patient and family as members of the care team.
questions.source_name: AHRQ — TeamSTEPPS 3.0
questions.source_detail: AHRQ describes TeamSTEPPS as an evidence-based framework for communication and teamwork among health care teams, including patients and family caregivers.

questions.stem: After a client's death, the donor registry shows documented first-person authorization for organ donation. A relative says, 'I am next of kin, so I can cancel it.' What should the nurse do?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Ask the family to vote on whether donation may proceed because documented donor authorization becomes advisory after death and must then be replaced by a new family consensus decision.","B":"Tell the closest relative that they alone can cancel any prior donor authorization because next-of-kin status automatically overrides the decedent's documented anatomical gift after death.","C":"Have the bedside nurse obtain new donation consent from the relative who is present before the organ procurement organization reviews the donor record and the legally valid authorization process in the case.","D":"Notify the organ procurement organization and follow the legal authorization process; documented first-person donor authorization is generally honored rather than replaced by family reauthorization."}}
questions.rationale: HRSA/OPTN describes documented first-person authorization as the individual's legally recognized anatomical gift. When such authorization exists, the donor's wishes are carried out if donation is medically possible. The organ procurement organization manages the authorization and donation process and supports the family; bedside staff should not create a new competing consent process.
questions.source_name: HRSA / OPTN — Ethics of Deceased Organ Donor Recovery
questions.source_detail: HRSA describes first-person authorization as the deceased individual's anatomical gift; surrogate authorization is used when no documentation of the individual's wishes exists.

questions.stem: A quality-improvement committee reviews its hospital's HCAHPS results. Which interpretation of the survey is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Treat HCAHPS as a direct measure of clinical outcomes such as mortality, readmissions, and complication rates rather than as a survey of the patient's hospital experience.","B":"Use HCAHPS to evaluate standardized patient-reported experience domains such as communication, staff responsiveness, care coordination, environment, and overall hospital rating.","C":"Interpret HCAHPS as a staff-satisfaction instrument because its primary purpose is to compare nurse and physician perceptions of workload, leadership, and compensation across hospitals.","D":"Use HCAHPS mainly to evaluate billing accuracy and insurance processing because financial experience is the principal domain used for public comparison of acute-care hospitals."}}
questions.rationale: CMS describes HCAHPS as a national, standardized, publicly reported survey of patients' perspectives on hospital care. It includes domains such as communication with nurses and doctors, staff responsiveness, care coordination, hospital environment, medication communication, discharge information, overall rating, and willingness to recommend.
questions.source_name: CMS — Hospital CAHPS (HCAHPS)
questions.source_detail: CMS defines HCAHPS as a standardized survey of patient perspectives on hospital care and lists its current patient-experience domains.

questions.stem: The nurse receives four requests at the same time. Which client should the nurse assess first?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"See the client awaiting routine discharge teaching first because completing scheduled education early prevents delays even when another assigned client has an acute change in condition.","B":"See the client requesting a PRN sleep medication first because comfort requests should take priority over new physiologic findings when both clients are currently on the same unit.","C":"See the client with new stridor and increasing work of breathing first because an acute airway problem threatens immediate stability and requires priority assessment and action.","D":"See the client with chronic knee pain rated 7/10 first because a high numeric pain score automatically outranks new airway or breathing deterioration in another assigned client."}}
questions.rationale: The 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan explicitly measures clinical judgment and the ability to take action on the highest-priority problem. New stridor with increasing work of breathing represents an immediate airway threat and therefore takes priority over routine teaching, a sleep-medication request, or stable chronic pain.
questions.source_name: NCSBN — 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
questions.source_detail: The 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan defines clinical judgment processes including recognizing cues, prioritizing hypotheses, and taking action on the highest-priority problem.

questions.stem: A toddler has a brief generalized febrile seizure. The shaking has stopped, but the child remains drowsy and is breathing spontaneously. What should the nurse do first?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Place the child on the side, maintain a safe airway position, assess breathing and responsiveness, and continue close observation while the child recovers from the seizure.","B":"Give oral fluids immediately to replace losses from fever because swallowing can be assumed to be safe once generalized shaking has stopped and the child is no longer convulsing.","C":"Restrain the child's arms and legs during the postictal period because limiting movement prevents another seizure while the temperature is being rechecked and treated.","D":"Insert an object between the teeth after the seizure to protect the tongue because oral injury remains the main immediate danger once the convulsive activity has ended."}}
questions.rationale: After a generalized febrile seizure, immediate priorities are safety, airway and breathing assessment, and recovery positioning. A drowsy child should not be given oral fluids until fully alert and able to swallow safely. Restraining the child or placing objects in the mouth does not prevent seizure injury and can cause harm.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Pediatrics — Febrile Seizures in Children / Seizure First Aid
questions.source_detail: AAP guidance emphasizes protecting the child from injury, maintaining the airway, and seeking evaluation after a febrile seizure; objects should not be placed in the mouth.

questions.stem: A child with suspected viral croup is being assessed. Which finding indicates the greatest need for urgent evaluation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A barky cough that occurs mainly when the child cries, with no stridor at rest and normal color, is the finding that most strongly indicates impending upper-airway failure.","B":"Mild hoarseness with a low-grade fever and comfortable breathing is the finding that most strongly indicates severe croup requiring emergency airway intervention.","C":"Intermittent cough with normal air movement and no retractions is the finding that most strongly indicates progressive airway obstruction from severe croup.","D":"Stridor at rest with retractions or increasing fatigue indicates more severe upper-airway obstruction and requires urgent evaluation rather than routine home observation."}}
questions.rationale: AAP guidance identifies a barky cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor as typical of croup. Stridor at rest, retractions, increasing work of breathing, fatigue, cyanosis, or inability to speak/drink indicate more severe upper-airway obstruction and require urgent evaluation.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Pediatrics — Croup in Young Children
questions.source_detail: AAP notes that stridor at rest and increasing breathing effort are signs of more severe croup that need medical evaluation.

questions.stem: A client reports abdominal pain that began near the umbilicus and migrated to the right lower quadrant with localized tenderness and low-grade fever. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Pain that remains localized to the epigastrium and improves after eating is most consistent with appendiceal inflammation progressing toward perforation and generalized peritonitis.","B":"Pain that migrated from the periumbilical area to the right lower quadrant with focal tenderness is compatible with acute appendicitis and warrants prompt surgical evaluation.","C":"Burning dysuria with suprapubic discomfort and urinary frequency is the classic progression of appendicitis because urinary symptoms usually precede right-lower-quadrant tenderness.","D":"Diffuse cramping relieved by defecation with no fever or focal tenderness is the pattern most concerning for acute appendicitis requiring immediate operative evaluation."}}
questions.rationale: Acute appendicitis classically begins with vague or periumbilical pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant as the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed. Localized right-lower-quadrant or McBurney-point tenderness, often with nausea or fever, warrants prompt evaluation because delayed diagnosis increases the risk of perforation and abscess.
questions.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Appendicitis
questions.source_detail: Current clinical review describes periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant and localized McBurney-point tenderness as classic appendicitis findings.

questions.stem: Several hours after cardiac surgery, a client develops hypotension, jugular venous distention, and muffled heart sounds. Which complication should the nurse suspect first?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The findings are most consistent with uncomplicated postoperative pain because hypotension after cardiac surgery commonly causes jugular venous distention without impaired filling.","B":"The findings suggest isolated left-sided heart failure because muffled heart sounds and rising venous pressure are expected when pulmonary congestion is the only problem.","C":"The combination of hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, and muffled heart sounds raises concern for cardiac tamponade and requires immediate escalation for evaluation.","D":"The findings are expected after cardiac surgery and can be observed until the next routine assessment because tamponade typically presents with hypertension and flat neck veins."}}
questions.rationale: Cardiac tamponade occurs when pericardial pressure impairs cardiac filling and output. Hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, and muffled heart sounds are concerning classic findings; after cardiac surgery, new hemodynamic deterioration requires immediate escalation because tamponade can rapidly become life-threatening.
questions.source_name: American Heart Association — Pericarditis Complications: Cardiac Tamponade
questions.source_detail: AHA describes tamponade as pressure from pericardial fluid that impairs filling and pumping and can cause a dangerous fall in blood pressure.

questions.stem: A critically ill client with severe sepsis begins oozing from IV sites while laboratory and clinical findings also suggest microvascular thrombosis. Which disorder best explains this combination?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Suspect disseminated intravascular coagulation because diffuse clotting activation can consume platelets and coagulation factors, producing both microthrombosis and bleeding.","B":"Suspect isolated immune thrombocytopenia because that disorder typically causes widespread fibrin microthrombi together with prolonged coagulation times and low fibrinogen.","C":"Interpret the findings as an expected inflammatory response because simultaneous oozing and microvascular thrombosis do not indicate pathologic coagulation activation in critical illness.","D":"Suspect uncomplicated vitamin K deficiency because it commonly produces diffuse microvascular thrombosis while also causing bleeding from vascular access sites in critical illness."}}
questions.rationale: DIC is a systemic activation of coagulation that produces fibrin deposition and microvascular thrombosis while consuming platelets and clotting factors, which can then cause clinically significant bleeding. A critically ill patient with both oozing and evidence of microthrombi fits this consumptive coagulopathy pattern.
questions.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation
questions.source_detail: DIC is characterized by widespread coagulation with consumption of platelets/factors, producing both thrombosis and bleeding.

questions.stem: A client with a crush injury has severe muscle pain, tea-colored urine, and a markedly elevated creatine kinase. Which complication should the nurse monitor for most closely?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The dark urine and high creatine kinase are most consistent with isolated hematuria, so kidney function and serum potassium are unlikely to change as muscle injury continues over the next several hours.","B":"The findings are expected after crush injury and do not require serial laboratory monitoring because creatine kinase elevation does not correlate with ongoing muscle breakdown.","C":"The main complication is progressive hypocalcemia without renal or cardiac consequences, so urine output and potassium monitoring are lower priorities during the early phase of crush injury.","D":"Rhabdomyolysis releases myoglobin and electrolytes, creating risk for acute kidney injury and dangerous hyperkalemia, so renal function, urine output, and potassium require close monitoring."}}
questions.rationale: Crush injury can cause rhabdomyolysis. CDC notes that muscle breakdown releases proteins and electrolytes, and rhabdomyolysis can lead to kidney injury or failure and dangerous arrhythmias. Dark urine plus markedly elevated CK warrants serial renal function, urine-output, and electrolyte monitoring, particularly potassium.
questions.source_name: CDC/NIOSH — Rhabdomyolysis
questions.source_detail: CDC identifies dark urine and elevated CK as key rhabdomyolysis findings and lists kidney damage and dangerous arrhythmias among major complications.

questions.stem: A client has a serum calcium of 12.8 mg/dL with constipation, intense thirst, fatigue, and new confusion. Which interpretation is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The calcium level is only mildly abnormal and the neurologic and gastrointestinal symptoms are unrelated, so no focused evaluation of the hypercalcemia or its cause is needed.","B":"The findings are more consistent with hypocalcemia because confusion, constipation, and thirst are typical manifestations of low calcium rather than elevated calcium in adults.","C":"The elevated calcium with constipation, thirst, and confusion is compatible with symptomatic hypercalcemia and warrants prompt evaluation of severity, cause, hydration status, and complications.","D":"The result establishes a single cause for the hypercalcemia, so assessment for malignancy, medications, parathyroid disease, renal factors, or dehydration is unnecessary in this client at this point."}}
questions.rationale: Hypercalcemia can produce gastrointestinal, renal, neuromuscular, and neurologic manifestations including constipation, polyuria/thirst, fatigue, and altered mental status. Symptomatic hypercalcemia requires prompt assessment of severity and etiology and evaluation of hydration, renal function, ECG risk, and the underlying cause.
questions.source_name: Endocrine Society — Hypercalcemia Guideline Resources
questions.source_detail: Endocrine Society guidance describes symptomatic hypercalcemia and emphasizes treatment based on severity and cause; severe hypercalcemia is a medical urgency.

questions.stem: A postoperative client receiving opioids is difficult to arouse and has a respiratory rate of 8/min. Which nursing response has the highest priority?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Give the next opioid dose as scheduled because respiratory rate alone is not clinically important when the client is sleeping and pain treatment has already been prescribed by the care team.","B":"Stop further opioid administration, stimulate and support ventilation as needed, and prepare for naloxone while activating the appropriate response for opioid-induced respiratory depression.","C":"Wait for the next routine vital-sign check because opioid-related sedation should be observed for several hours before the care team considers dose withholding or reversal.","D":"Administer a sedative to reduce agitation during stimulation because combining sedatives with opioids improves respiratory drive while the client becomes progressively more alert."}}
questions.rationale: A difficult-to-arouse client with a respiratory rate of 8/min after opioids has clinically significant opioid-induced respiratory/CNS depression. The opioid should be withheld, airway and ventilation supported as needed, and naloxone prepared/administered according to the emergency response. Naloxone labeling specifically indicates reversal of opioid respiratory depression.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Naloxone Hydrochloride Injection
questions.source_detail: Updated 2026 naloxone labeling indicates reversal of opioid-induced respiratory depression and requires supportive ventilation/resuscitative measures when needed.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old client has reduced muscle mass and is prescribed a medication that is primarily eliminated by the kidneys. Which dosing principle is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use an appropriate estimate of kidney function and the drug's renal-dosing guidance rather than relying on serum creatinine alone, because reduced muscle mass can mask impaired clearance.","B":"Use the same dose as in a younger adult whenever serum creatinine is within the laboratory reference range, because aging does not meaningfully change renal drug elimination.","C":"Increase the starting dose of renally cleared drugs in older adults because lower nephron mass increases drug distribution and usually requires more medication to reach therapeutic levels.","D":"Base renal dosing primarily on chronological age without considering weight, kidney-function estimates, indication, or the specific medication's pharmacokinetic characteristics."}}
questions.rationale: Kidney function commonly declines with age, and reduced muscle mass can make serum creatinine appear deceptively normal despite reduced filtration. Renally cleared drugs should therefore be dosed using the medication's specific renal guidance and an appropriate estimate of kidney function, not age or serum creatinine alone.
questions.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Drug Clearance and Renal Dosing in Older Adults
questions.source_detail: Clinical pharmacology references describe age-related decreases in renal filtration and the need to adjust renally eliminated drugs according to kidney function/creatinine clearance.

questions.stem: A client who is not taking anticoagulants has a markedly prolonged prothrombin time (PT). Which interpretation is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A prolonged PT primarily measures platelet adhesion and aggregation, so the result most directly indicates a platelet-function disorder rather than a coagulation-factor abnormality.","B":"A prolonged PT primarily reflects the intrinsic pathway, making factor VIII and IX abnormalities the most direct explanation for the result when anticoagulants are not being used.","C":"A prolonged PT directly measures red-cell production, so the result most directly indicates impaired erythropoiesis rather than a defect involving coagulation factors.","D":"A prolonged PT reflects abnormalities in the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways and can occur with vitamin K deficiency, liver dysfunction, or coagulation-factor deficiency."}}
questions.rationale: PT evaluates the tissue-factor/extrinsic and common coagulation pathways and is standardized as INR for many clinical uses. Prolongation can occur with vitamin K deficiency, liver synthetic dysfunction, factor deficiencies, and anticoagulant effects. PT does not directly measure platelet function, red-cell production, or the intrinsic pathway measured by aPTT.
questions.source_name: MedlinePlus / NLM — Prothrombin Time and INR
questions.source_detail: PT measures time to clot formation through a different portion of the coagulation system than PTT and is used in evaluation of bleeding/coagulation disorders and warfarin effect.

questions.stem: A client has a markedly elevated C-reactive protein (CRP). Which interpretation of this result is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A markedly elevated CRP identifies the exact infectious organism causing the client's illness, so culture or other diagnostic testing is unnecessary once the CRP result is known.","B":"A markedly elevated CRP specifically diagnoses an autoimmune disorder because infection, tissue injury, malignancy, and other inflammatory conditions do not meaningfully increase this marker.","C":"CRP is a nonspecific marker of inflammation that can rise with infection, injury, autoimmune disease, or other inflammatory states and must be interpreted with the overall clinical picture.","D":"CRP is primarily a marker of kidney filtration, so an elevated value should be interpreted as evidence of reduced glomerular filtration rather than evidence of systemic inflammation."}}
questions.rationale: CRP is produced by the liver in response to inflammation. An elevated CRP is nonspecific: it can accompany infection, tissue injury, autoimmune disease, and many other inflammatory conditions. The result must be interpreted with the history, examination, and other tests; it does not identify a specific diagnosis or organism.
questions.source_name: MedlinePlus / NLM — C-Reactive Protein Test
questions.source_detail: MedlinePlus describes CRP as a blood marker that rises in response to inflammation from infection, injury, autoimmune disease and other causes.

questions.stem: A nonpregnant adult with diabetes has an A1C of 9.5%. Which interpretation best reflects current glycemic-goal guidance?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An A1C of 9.5% is within the usual target for most nonpregnant adults, so treatment changes are generally unnecessary unless the client also reports recurrent hypoglycemia or symptoms.","B":"An A1C of 9.5% indicates glycemia well above the usual goal for many nonpregnant adults, but the treatment target should still be individualized to health status, preferences, and hypoglycemia risk.","C":"An A1C of 9.5% mainly indicates recurrent hypoglycemia because higher A1C values reflect excessive time below range rather than prolonged exposure to elevated glucose levels over several recent months.","D":"An A1C of 9.5% cannot provide useful information about recent glycemic exposure because A1C is used only to diagnose diabetes and not to monitor ongoing treatment effectiveness over time."}}
questions.rationale: The ADA 2026 Standards state that an A1C goal below 7% is appropriate for many nonpregnant adults, while goals should be individualized according to comorbidity, functional status, treatment burden, and hypoglycemia risk. An A1C of 9.5% is therefore substantially above the usual target for many adults, but treatment decisions remain individualized.
questions.source_name: American Diabetes Association — Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026: Glycemic Goals
questions.source_detail: ADA 2026 recommends A1C <7% for many nonpregnant adults while emphasizing individualized goals and deintensification when treatment harms exceed benefits.

questions.stem: An adult client's BMI is 32 kg/m². Which interpretation is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A BMI of 32 kg/m² falls in the CDC class 1 obesity screening category, but BMI should be interpreted with other clinical factors rather than used as a stand-alone diagnosis of health.","B":"A BMI of 32 kg/m² falls in the overweight category because obesity begins only at 35 kg/m² for adults and the lower threshold is used only in pediatric growth charts.","C":"A BMI of 32 kg/m² establishes the presence and severity of metabolic disease by itself, so laboratory findings, body composition, history, and other risk factors add little information.","D":"A BMI of 32 kg/m² is considered a healthy-weight value for adults because BMI categories depend mainly on age and sex rather than standard adult screening thresholds."}}
questions.rationale: CDC classifies adult BMI 30.0 to less than 35.0 kg/m² as Class 1 obesity. CDC also emphasizes that BMI is a screening measure rather than a stand-alone diagnosis of health or disease and should be considered with medical history, physical findings, behaviors, and other risk factors.
questions.source_name: CDC — Adult BMI Categories
questions.source_detail: CDC: adult BMI 30.0–34.9 is Class 1 obesity; BMI is a screening measure and should be interpreted with other health information.

questions.stem: A hospitalized client has a high Morse Fall Scale score and several modifiable fall-risk factors. Which interpretation should guide the nurse's plan?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A high Morse score means every patient should receive the same fall-prevention bundle because the total score alone determines which interventions are effective for that individual.","B":"A high Morse score eliminates the need for repeat assessment because once high risk is documented, changes in medications, cognition, gait, or environment no longer alter the plan.","C":"A low Morse score guarantees that the patient will not fall, so staff can omit individualized prevention measures even when new dizziness or unsteady gait develops later.","D":"A higher Morse score indicates greater fall risk, but prevention should still target the patient's specific risk factors and be updated when the clinical situation changes."}}
questions.rationale: A higher Morse score indicates greater fall risk, but AHRQ's fall-prevention work warns against using the score alone to give every high-risk patient the same interventions. Effective prevention identifies patient-specific risk factors and implements a tailored plan that is reassessed when medications, gait, cognition, or clinical status change.
questions.source_name: AHRQ — Fall TIPS / Preventing Falls in Hospitals
questions.source_detail: AHRQ supports formal fall-risk assessment plus patient-specific interventions and notes that a score alone should not replace individualized clinical judgment.

questions.stem: A postoperative client can bear weight but is mildly unsteady when first walking to the bathroom. Which nursing approach provides the safest hands-on assistance during ambulation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use a properly fitted gait belt and walk beside the client, maintaining a secure grasp safely while allowing the client to participate in the movement.","B":"Wrap a folded bedsheet around the client's waist and use it as a transfer handle because improvised fabric provides support equivalent to a gait belt.","C":"Hold the client under both arms during walking because axillary support gives the nurse better control if the client's knees suddenly begin to buckle.","D":"Ask the client to hold onto the nurse's neck or shoulders because direct upper-body contact provides the most stable support during an unexpected loss of balance."}}
questions.rationale: A gait belt can provide a secure handhold for a client who can participate in standing and walking but needs hands-on assistance. It should be properly fitted and used according to mobility assessment and facility policy. Pulling under the arms or having the client hang from staff creates injury risk.
questions.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Nursing Fundamentals: Transfers and Ambulation
questions.source_detail: Safe ambulation uses an appropriate transfer/gait belt when indicated and avoids unsafe improvised or axillary pulling techniques.

questions.stem: A client recovering from shoulder surgery can move the affected arm through part of the prescribed range but needs assistance to complete the motion. Which exercise description is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Passive range of motion means the client contracts the muscles independently while the nurse observes the joint without assisting or guiding the movement.","B":"Active range of motion means the nurse moves the joint through the prescribed arc while the client remains relaxed and contributes no muscle effort.","C":"Active-assisted range of motion means the client initiates the movement and receives help to complete the prescribed range that cannot yet be reached alone.","D":"Resistive range of motion means the joint is moved without muscle contraction so mobility can be maintained while the affected extremity remains completely relaxed."}}
questions.rationale: Active ROM is performed by the client; passive ROM is performed for a client who cannot move the joint independently. Active-assisted ROM is appropriate when the client can initiate movement but lacks sufficient strength or mobility to complete the prescribed range alone.
questions.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Nursing Fundamentals: Range of Motion
questions.source_detail: Active-assisted ROM combines the client's voluntary movement with assistance to complete the available prescribed range.

questions.stem: A client with a new colostomy reports repeated pouch leakage and burning of the skin directly around the stoma. Which teaching best addresses the likely cause while protecting peristomal skin?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Apply an oily moisturizing cream under the skin barrier at each change because a lubricated surface improves adhesive contact and prevents effluent from reaching the skin.","B":"Re-measure the stoma and fit the barrier opening closely around its base, changing the system promptly when leakage or burning occurs rather than reinforcing the leak.","C":"Cut the barrier opening noticeably larger than the stoma so pressure is avoided, even if a rim of peristomal skin remains exposed to stool beneath the pouching system.","D":"Keep a leaking pouch in place until the routine change day because frequent replacement damages skin more than continued exposure to stool beneath a loosened barrier."}}
questions.rationale: Leakage allows stool to contact peristomal skin and is a common cause of irritation. WOCN guidance recommends a barrier opening that fits closely around the stoma base and prompt pouch-system change when leakage, burning, or itching occurs; simply reinforcing a leak or leaving exposed skin under an oversized opening can worsen injury.
questions.source_name: WOCN — Peristomal Skin Assessment Guide for Consumers
questions.source_detail: WOCN advises routinely measuring the stoma, sizing the barrier opening closely around the stoma base, and changing the system promptly for leakage, burning, or itching.

questions.stem: An older adult removes complete dentures for nighttime care. Which instruction best protects the dentures while also supporting effective cleaning and storage?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Brush the dentures with a stiff brush and abrasive whitening toothpaste, then leave them completely dry overnight so the acrylic surface can fully air out safely.","B":"Rinse the dentures with very hot water before storage because high temperatures disinfect the appliance without changing its shape or surface properties.","C":"Store the dentures dry in an uncovered cup and clean them only when visible debris appears because daily soaking can weaken properly fitted denture material over time.","D":"Clean the dentures with an appropriate nonabrasive method, avoid hot or boiling water, and keep them in water or denture solution when they are not being worn."}}
questions.rationale: Dentures should be cleaned regularly with a method that does not damage the material. ADA guidance warns against hot or boiling water because it can warp dentures and recommends keeping dentures in water or an appropriate solution when not worn so they do not dry out.
questions.source_name: American Dental Association — Denture Care and Maintenance
questions.source_detail: ADA guidance supports daily nonabrasive cleaning, avoiding hot or boiling water, and keeping dentures moist in water or denture solution when not worn.

questions.stem: A client with no history of skin cancer asks which daily habits provide the most effective general protection from ultraviolet exposure. Which teaching is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use sunscreen mainly on clear summer days because cloud cover blocks most clinically important ultraviolet exposure and protective clothing adds little benefit.","B":"Use broad-spectrum, water-resistant SPF 30 or higher on exposed skin, seek shade, wear sun-protective clothing, and reapply sunscreen as directed when outdoors.","C":"Use indoor tanning instead of outdoor tanning because artificial ultraviolet exposure produces cosmetic pigmentation without meaningfully increasing skin-cancer risk.","D":"Skip sunscreen on darker skin tones because naturally higher melanin prevents clinically important ultraviolet injury and makes other sun-protection measures unnecessary."}}
questions.rationale: AAD recommends a layered sun-protection strategy: seek shade, wear protective clothing, and apply broad-spectrum, water-resistant SPF 30 or higher to exposed skin, with reapplication as directed. UV exposure occurs on cloudy days and affects people of all skin tones; tanning beds also expose users to carcinogenic UV radiation.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Dermatology — Skin Cancer Prevention
questions.source_detail: AAD recommends broad-spectrum, water-resistant SPF 30+ sunscreen, shade, protective clothing, and reapplication approximately every 2 hours or after swimming/sweating.

questions.stem: A parent asks when a healthy infant should first establish routine preventive dental care. Which recommendation is most consistent with current pediatric dental guidance?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Schedule the first dental visit when all primary teeth have erupted, because earlier visits do not provide meaningful preventive benefit before the full dentition is present.","B":"Wait until the child begins preschool unless pain, trauma, or visible decay occurs, because routine dental risk assessment is unnecessary during infancy.","C":"Establish a dental home within 6 months after the first tooth erupts and no later than 12 months of age so prevention and caries-risk assessment begin early.","D":"Delay the first visit until the child can cooperate with a full examination, usually around age 3, while relying on primary-care visits for all earlier oral-health needs."}}
questions.rationale: AAPD recommends establishing a dental home within 6 months after eruption of the first tooth and no later than 12 months of age. Early visits allow caries-risk assessment, preventive counseling, oral-hygiene guidance, and dietary counseling rather than waiting for symptoms or a full primary dentition.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry — Early Childhood Caries Policy
questions.source_detail: AAPD recommends establishment of a dental home within 6 months of eruption of the first tooth and no later than 12 months of age.

questions.stem: A dependent hospitalized client must be transferred from bed to chair, and the task would require substantial manual lifting by staff. Which approach best reflects current safe-patient-handling guidance?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use an appropriate mechanical lift or other assistive device with trained staff, selecting equipment that safely matches the client's weight, mobility, and transfer needs.","B":"Use a manual two-person lift with both nurses bending at the knees because correct body mechanics make heavy patient lifting acceptably safe without assistive equipment.","C":"Have the strongest staff member perform the lift quickly while the client holds the worker's shoulders because reducing transfer time is the main way to prevent back injury.","D":"Use a drawsheet as the sole lifting device for the full body weight because fabric-assisted manual lifting eliminates the ergonomic hazards associated with patient transfers."}}
questions.rationale: Traditional 'good body mechanics' do not make heavy manual patient lifting safe. NIOSH recommends safe-patient-handling and mobility programs using appropriate mechanical or assistive technology selected for the patient and task, with trained staff. This reduces risk to both workers and patients.
questions.source_name: CDC/NIOSH — Safe Patient Handling and Mobility
questions.source_detail: NIOSH recommends safe-patient-handling programs and assistive lifting devices because manual patient handling is a major cause of musculoskeletal injury.

questions.stem: The spouse of a client with advanced cancer begins crying, discussing expected changes after the client's death, and making funeral plans while the client is still alive. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The behavior indicates complicated grief because planning for a death before it occurs is abnormal and generally requires psychiatric treatment before bereavement begins promptly.","B":"The spouse is demonstrating denial because acknowledging the possibility of death while planning for it shows an inability to recognize the client's actual prognosis.","C":"The response is evidence of major depression because sadness before a death is not considered part of normal grief and should be treated as a psychiatric disorder.","D":"The spouse may be experiencing anticipatory grief, which can occur before an expected death and can include sadness, preparation, and emotional adjustment to impending loss."}}
questions.rationale: Anticipatory grief can begin before an expected death and may involve sadness, preparation, worry, and adjustment to impending loss. It does not occur in everyone and should not automatically be pathologized as depression or complicated grief; support is based on the person's needs and functioning.
questions.source_name: National Cancer Institute — Grief, Bereavement, and Loss
questions.source_detail: NCI identifies anticipatory grief as grief that occurs before an expected death and may be experienced by the dying person or family.

questions.stem: During a routine primary-care visit, an asymptomatic 29-year-old woman is privately screened for intimate partner violence. Which statement best reflects current USPSTF guidance?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Routine screening is recommended only when physical injuries are visible because screening asymptomatic women without signs of abuse has no demonstrated preventive benefit.","B":"Screen women of reproductive age, including pregnant and postpartum women, and connect those who screen positive with appropriate multicomponent support services and follow-up.","C":"A positive screening response automatically establishes a criminal case and requires the nurse to report every adult disclosure to law enforcement in every U.S. jurisdiction without exception.","D":"Screening should be avoided in primary care because intimate partner violence assessment is recommended only in emergency departments after an assault has already occurred."}}
questions.rationale: USPSTF recommends IPV screening for women of reproductive age, including pregnant and postpartum women, and provision or referral to multicomponent interventions with ongoing support when screening is positive. Screening does not itself create a criminal case, and mandatory-reporting duties vary by jurisdiction and circumstance.
questions.source_name: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force — Intimate Partner Violence Screening
questions.source_detail: The June 2025 USPSTF recommendation is Grade B for screening women of reproductive age, including pregnant and postpartum women, with referral/provision of multicomponent interventions for positive screens.
